data.narrative: The student moved from treating risk as a vague feeling to using a concrete framework that separated integration, novelty, dependency, scale, and non-technical readiness blockers. They built a risk-ordered plan, then adapted it calmly when payments became a business blocker by preserving the interface contract and keeping the rest of the system moving.

dimension_scores.observation: They recognized that the original payment requirement carried an unstated business assumption and later reclassified it correctly when the blocker was revealed.
dimension_scores.evidence: They wrote that the Stripe issue was 'a business/legal readiness risk, not just a technical risk' and noted that legal/payment readiness can invalidate a technically sound plan.

dimension_scores.observation: They cleanly separated what was truly blocked by payments from what could still proceed and preserved the plan shape instead of freezing the whole system.
dimension_scores.evidence: They split 'Truly blocked: real Stripe integration, live money movement, commission on real transactions, refunds' from 'Not blocked: payment contract, transaction data model, pricing UI, booking flow calling a payment boundary.'

dimension_scores.observation: They used multiple risk types appropriately, front-loaded the biggest unknowns, and responded correctly when the highest-risk item turned out to be blocked for non-technical reasons.
dimension_scores.evidence: Top risks were identified as Payment Processing (5, integration/dependency), Booking Flow (4, novelty/dependency), and Search & Browse (3, scale/dependency), and they chose a spike first because it 'can save weeks of building on a broken assumption.'

dimension_scores.observation: Their payment stub contract is precise enough for another engineer to implement without follow-up questions.
dimension_scores.evidence: They defined `processPayment(bookingId, amount, paymentMethod) -> { status, transactionId }` and specified that development should return fake success/failure and log the request while preserving the contract.

dimension_scores.observation: When the payment blocker appeared, they adapted immediately and pragmatically instead of trying to solve the wrong problem with code.
dimension_scores.evidence: They said real payment work 'drops out of the near-term implementation plan and becomes an external blocker' and replaced it with 'Payment Interface Contract + Stub' while moving booking and availability earlier.

dimension_scores.observation: They thought ahead to the eventual swap from stubbed implementation to live integration and preserved a stable seam for the rest of the system.
dimension_scores.evidence: They explicitly said to 'replace only the implementation with Stripe while keeping the booking contract stable.'

strengths: Strong risk framing: they stopped equating risk with difficulty and used concrete categories to justify the build order.
Strong non-technical adaptation: when the blocker moved outside the codebase, they escalated it properly instead of inventing a technical workaround.
Strong contract design: the stubbed payment interface preserved team flow and future integration flexibility.
data.recommendation: In Module 4, keep this same discipline by turning the reordered plan into thin vertical slices that prove real user value without dragging in unnecessary surrounding work.
